newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan CPC says fix at hand for Ecuador venture.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan CPC says fix at hand for Ecuador venture.

text.p: Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Friday it and its partner in an Ecuadoran joint venture had devised a solution to a dispute with Quito over crude production and hoped for Ecuador's approval.
The plan was set during a Taiwan visit by John Schmid, president of Maxus Ecuador, a subsidiary of Maxus Energy Corp of Dallas and lead partner in the troubled venture.

"We reached a solution plan with Schmid that should satisfy (the) Ecuador government's demand to share the joint venture's production," Chinese Petroleum vice president Hsieh Shih-hsiung told Reuters.
Hsieh said he hoped Ecuador would accept the plan, which first needed Taiwan government approval.
Ecuador in August banned Maxus from operating the venture in the country's Block 16 Amazon oil field, saying it failed to share profits to benefit Ecuador's state oil firm Petroecuador.

Under the new plan, production from the venture to explore for and extract Ecuadoran crude would be split among the partners and Ecuador along ratios that would depend on levels of production, Hsieh said.
"Production sharing would not be based on a fixed number but would follow production volume," Hsieh said.

He declined to give details of the scheme, which would replace the venture's original profit-sharing service contract with Ecuador. Under the old arrangement, the venture was obliged to share profits but not to hand over oil to Ecuador.

Ecuadoran energy and mining minister Alfredo Adum has proposed that the joint venture, which is operated by Maxus, should "hand over to the Ecuadoran state 29 barrels of oil for every 100 barrels it produces".

Maxus holds a leading 35 percent of the venture, followed by Chinese Petroleum at 31 percent. Nomeco Ecuador Oil has 14 percent and Canam Offshore Ltd and Murphy Ecuador Oil Co each hold 10 percent stakes.
Hsieh said the partners' ownership stakes would not change under the new arrangement, but that the term of the contract with Ecuador would have to be extended.
"We would need to add another three or four years to the contract to cover the shared profit," he said.
Hsieh said exploration in Ecuador was still under way despite the government decree.
